JOINT STATEMENT
The Government of the Federal Democratic Republic 
of Ethiopia and the United Nations Development 
System (UNDS) in Ethiopia are honored to present 
the United Nations Sustainable Development 
Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF) 2025–2030. 
This Cooperation Framework represents a shared 
commitment to advancing Ethiopia’s development 
priorities and achieving the Sustainable Development 
Goals (SDGs) by 2030.
The UNSDCF is the primary instrument for 
planning and implementing the United Nations’ 
development activities in Ethiopia. It reflects the 
principles of the 2018 UNDS reform, which aims to 
enhance coordination, transparency, and impact in 
supporting countries to achieve the 2030 Agenda 
for Sustainable Development. Rooted in Ethiopia’s 
Ten-Year Development Plan (TYDP) (2021–2030), 
the UNSDCF aligns with the global 2030 Agenda and 
Africa Agenda 2063, ensuring coherence between 
national, regional, and global priorities.
This Cooperation Framework is the result of an 
inclusive and consultative process, engaging the 
Government of Ethiopia (GoE), civil society, private 
sector, youth, vulnerable groups, and development 
partners. It reflects our collective ambition to address 
Ethiopia’s most pressing challenges, including 
conflict, climate shocks, economic pressures, and 
governance deficits, while unlocking opportunities 
for inclusive and sustainable growth.
The UNSDCF 2025–2030 is built around five strategic 
priorities that address Ethiopia’s development 
aspirations:
Peace and Governance: Strengthening 
institutions, fostering social cohesion, 
and advancing human rights to ensure a 
peaceful, just, and democratic society.
Inclusive Economic Growth, Food 
Systems, and Energy: Promoting 
sustainable livelihoods, creating decent 
jobs, and ensuring access to affordable 
green energy for all.
Social Services and Protection: 
Enhancing equitable access to quality 
education, healthcare, and social 
protection systems, leaving no one 
behind.
Environmental Sustainability and 
Resilience: Building climate resilience, 
reducing disaster risks, and promoting 
sustainable natural resource 
management.
Gender Equality and Empowerment 
of Women and Youth: Addressing 
systemic barriers and empowering 
women and young people to fully 
participate in all aspects of society.
The United Nations will leverage its global expertise, 
partnerships, and convening power to support 
Ethiopia in achieving these transformative goals. 
By fostering collaboration, mobilizing resources, 
and promoting innovative solutions, the UN will 
work alongside the Government and stakeholders 
to accelerate progress toward Ethiopia’s vision of 
becoming an African Beacon of Prosperity.
This Cooperation Framework is more than a 
roadmap; it is a testament to our shared commitment 
to inclusivity, equality, and sustainability. It prioritizes 
the needs of the most vulnerable, ensuring that no 
one is left behind. It also emphasizes accountability, 
transparency, and results-oriented implementation, 
ensuring that our collective efforts deliver measurable 
and lasting impact.
As we embark on this journey together, we reaffirm 
our shared vision of an equitable, peaceful, and 
prosperous Ethiopia, driven by self-reliance and 
resilience. Together, we will build a future where every 
citizen has the opportunity to thrive and exercise 
their rights.
Signed in partnership and solidarity,
Government of Ethiopia United Nations

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
The Ethiopia United Nations Sustainable Development 
Cooperation Framework (2025–2030) outlines the 
strategic partnership between the United Nations and 
Ethiopia to accelerate progress toward the country’s 
development priorities and the SDGs. Anchored on 
Ethiopia’s Ten-Year Development Plan (2021–2030) 
and aligned with Agenda 2030 for Sustainable 
Development and Africa Agenda 2063: The Africa 
We Want, the framework envisions an equitable, 
peaceful, and prosperous Ethiopia, driven by selfreliance and resilience, where no one is left behind, 
and sustainable development is achieved for all by 
2030. At the heart of this Cooperation Framework is 
a bold ambition to achieve transformative results by 
2030. It seeks to end aid dependency for the most 
vulnerable populations by fostering self-reliance 
and creating sustainable livelihoods. It aims to 
achieve food security through increased agricultural 
productivity and the local production of nutritious 
food, ensuring that all Ethiopians have access to 
sufficient and healthy diets. The framework also 
envisions a fully digitized public service system, 
enabling equitable access to essential goods and 
services for all citizens. Furthermore, it aspires to 
ensure universal access to clean energy and water, 
improving the quality of life for all Ethiopians and 
laying the foundation for sustainable development.
To achieve these transformative results, the 
Cooperation Framework adopts a strategic approach 
that accelerates progress through six transformational 
SDG transitions, addressing Ethiopia’s development 
priorities while tackling the root causes of recurrent 
humanitarian needs and promoting durable solutions. 
It emphasizes fostering joint strategic and innovative 
interventions that deliver scalable and catalytic 
impact, embedding equality, inclusion, human rights, 
and sustainability as cross-cutting principles in all 
interventions. Strengthening accountability and 
results-oriented implementation is central to this 
approach, ensuring that progress is measurable and 
impactful.
The Cooperation Framework is structured around 
five strategic priorities that address Ethiopia’s most 
pressing challenges and unlock opportunities for 
sustainable development. It focuses on strengthening 
peace and governance by strengthening institutions 
and governance mechanisms, including their 
interface with civil society and affected populations, 
and promoting evidence-based policymaking 
to advance peace, justice, and human rights. It 
promotes inclusive economic growth, sustainable 
food systems, and access to affordable green energy, 
ensuring that all Ethiopians benefit from resilient and 
sustainable economic development. The framework 
also prioritizes enhancing equitable access to quality 
social services and social protection systems, 
ensuring that no one is left behind. It scales up green 
economy investments and climate resilience to reduce 
environmental risks and crises, while promoting 
gender equality and non-discrimination based on 
gender, age, ability, and other factors, and fostering 
an enabling environment for all sectors of society, 
including women and youth, to fully participate in and 
benefit from all aspects of society.
The Cooperation Framework was developed through 
an inclusive and evidence-based consultative 
process, engaging the Government, civil society, 
private sector, youth, vulnerable groups, and 
international development partners. It reflects 
Ethiopia’s ambition to address key development 
challenges, including structural macro-economic 
imbalances, the recurrence of humanitarian crises 
mainly driven by conflict, climate, economic shocks, 
and displacement, and governance deficits and 
bottlenecks, while leveraging opportunities to foster 
lasting peace and achieve sustainable development 
for all. Ethiopia has made significant progress in 
recent decades, including rapid economic growth 
and improved living standards. However, overlapping 
crises since 2020 have strained this progress, 
increasing food insecurity, poverty, and inequalities. 
The Cooperation Framework aims to address these 
challenges by fostering resilience, promoting inclusive 
development, and ensuring that no one is left behind.
The United Nations will leverage its global expertise, 
partnerships, and convening power to support Ethiopia 
in achieving these transformative goals. By fostering

CHAPTER 1: 
COUNTRY 
PROGRESS 
TOWARD THE 
2030 AGENDA 
Photo: A UN Project in collaboration with the Korea Forest Service is empowering local farmers in Ethiopia to restore their land, 
secure sustainable incomes, and combat climate change. © UNEP12 UNSDCF ETHIOPIA 2025-2030 UNSDCF ETHIOPIA 2025-2030 13
Ethiopia is at a pivotal moment in its development 
journey, navigating a complex landscape of challenges 
and opportunities. With an estimated population of 
129.7 million in 2024, Ethiopia is the second most 
populous nation in Africa and a country of immense 
diversity, with over 80 nationalities, languages, and 
unique cultural features. Over the past two decades, 
Ethiopia has achieved remarkable developmental 
progress, with real Gross Domestic Product growth 
averaging 10% annually from 2004 to 2019. This 
growth lifted millions out of poverty, improved key 
social indicators, and positioned Ethiopia as one 
of Africa’s top-performing economies during that 
period. These achievements reflect the country’s 
commitment to sound economic management, 
development planning, and inclusive growth.
However, like many countries, Ethiopia has faced 
challenges in sustaining this momentum. Since 
2020, a confluence of pre-existing overlapping 
crises—including conflict, climate-induced disasters, 
economic pressures, and the COVID-19 pandemic—
has slowed economic growth and strained public 
services. As of 2024, an estimated 21.4 million 
people required humanitarian assistance, including 
3.6 million internally displaced persons (IDPs). Food 
insecurity remains a critical challenge, exacerbated 
by climate shocks, limited agricultural productivity, 
and environmental degradation. Groups in vulnerable 
situations, including women, children, persons 
with disabilities, migrant returnees, and IDPs, have 
been disproportionately affected, facing barriers to 
accessing basic services, education, and economic 
opportunities.
Despite these challenges, Ethiopia has demonstrated 
remarkable resilience and remains steadfast in its 
commitment to achieving its development priorities. 
The GoE is implementing the TYDP for 2021–2030, 
which envisions Ethiopia as an “African Beacon 
of Prosperity.” The plan targets an average annual 
economic growth rate of 10.2%, aiming to double per 
capita income and reduce the poverty rate from 19% 
to 7% by 2030. The SDGs are fully integrated into the 
TYDP, with significant budget allocations to pro-poor 
sectors and a focus on inclusive economic growth, 
environmental protection, and social inclusion. 
These efforts reflect Ethiopia’s strong commitment 
to sustainable development and its determination to 
leave no one behind.
Ethiopia’s progress toward the SDGs has been uneven, 
reflecting the complexity of the challenges it faces. 
According to the 2024 SDG Index, Ethiopia ranks 
145th out of 167 countries. The country has achieved 
two SDGs—SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption 
and Production) and SDG 13 (Climate Action)—and 
made moderate progress on SDG 1 (No Poverty), 
SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-being), and SDG 5 
(Gender Equality). However, progress on other goals 
has been slower, with limited data available for SDG 
10 (Reduced Inequalities) and SDG 14 (Life Below 
Water). Overall, 22.2% of SDG targets are on track 
to be achieved by 2030, while 52.4% show limited 
progress, and 25.4% have regressed. These trends 
underscore the importance of addressing structural 
challenges while leveraging Ethiopia’s strengths to 
accelerate progress.
Unlocking Opportunities for Transformation
Ethiopia’s challenges also present significant 
opportunities for transformative change. The 
country’s strong tradition of development planning, 
coupled with its ambitious reform agenda and 
resilient population, provides a solid foundation for 
unlocking its vast potential. The Common Country 
Analysis (CCA) highlights several key opportunities 
that can accelerate progress toward the SDGs.
Ethiopia’s legal and policy frameworks reflect its 
commitment to achieving the SDGs. This is evident 
in the government’s ongoing efforts to implement 
economic reforms, transform agriculture, and 
promote renewable energy. Efforts to improve service 
delivery are being combined with the potential of 
digital solutions, while the promotion of a green 
economy is creating decent jobs and expanding 
energy access to underserved communities. Gender 
equality remains a central priority, with initiatives 
aimed at empowering women and ensuring their full 
participation in Ethiopia’s development.

Strong partnerships at the global, continental, and 
regional levels also provide a critical opportunity to 
support Ethiopia’s sustainable development efforts. 
Ethiopia’s engagement with platforms such as 
the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), 
Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa (BRICS), 
Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), 
and Common Market for Eastern and Southern 
Africa (COMESA), as well as its collaboration with 
bilateral and multilateral partners, underscores the 
importance of collective action. Domestically, the 
private sector holds significant untapped potential 
to contribute to Ethiopia’s development goals, 
particularly in areas such as job creation, innovation, 
and investment.
Ethiopia’s abundant renewable energy resources 
offer a unique opportunity to build a green economy. 
The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, which is the 
largest hydropower project in Africa, exemplifies 
Ethiopia’s commitment to sustainable energy 
development. Investments in renewable energy 
infrastructure, including solar and wind, are helping 
to reduce reliance on fossil fuels, expand access to 
electricity, support industrialization and accelerate 
regional power integration.
The country’s young and dynamic population reflects 
a significant youth bulge that can drive economic 
growth if supported by investments in education, 
healthcare, and job creation programs such as the 
Youth Revolving Fund and Technical and Vocational 
Education and Training (TVET) centers are critical 
for harnessing this potential. Prioritizing education, 
healthcare access, and employment opportunities 
will be critical to harnessing the potential of 
Ethiopia’s youth and laying the groundwork for future 
demographic dividends.

Advancements in technology provide a 
significant opportunity to introduce and improve 
systems and practices that are more effective 
and efficient. Ethiopia’s digital development 
programs, including Digital Ethiopia 2025, aim to 
create an inclusive economy and society driven 
by technology. By leveraging digital solutions, 
Ethiopia can enhance service delivery, expand 
access to underserved populations, and drive 
innovation in key sectors such as education, 
healthcare, and agriculture.
While Ethiopia faces complex development 
challenges, these also present significant 
opportunities for progress and transformation. By 
addressing the root causes of conflict, inequality, 
and vulnerability, fostering inclusive dialogue to 
promote peaceful coexistence, and strengthening 
institutions to effectively respond to citizens’ 
needs, Ethiopia can build a strong foundation for 
sustainable and inclusive growth, aligned with its 
human rights obligations. Strengthening governance 
and accountability measures, fostering inclusive 
economic transformation, improving access to social 
services, promoting environmental sustainability, 
and empowering women and young people will be 
critical to achieving the SDGs and the country’s 
national development priorities, while preventing and 
addressing conflicts.
With sustained efforts and international support, 
Ethiopia has the potential to transition from a 
cycle of dependency to resilience and self-reliance. 
By focusing on inclusive development, localized 
implementation, and innovative solutions, Ethiopia 
can chart a path toward a peaceful, prosperous, and 
sustainable future—one where all citizens have the 
opportunity to thrive and exercise their rights.16 UNSDCF ETHIOPIA 2025-2030 UNSDCF ETHIOPIA 2025-2030 17

2.1 From CCA to Cooperation 
Framework Priorities
The Cooperation Framework’s strategic priorities for 
2025–2030 were identified through a consultative, 
evidence-based process involving the GoE, the Ethiopia 
UN Country Team (UNCT), development partners, civil 
society, and other stakeholders. This process was 
guided by the CCA, which provided a comprehensive 
assessment of Ethiopia’s development landscape, 
including progress toward the SDGs, persistent 
challenges, and emerging opportunities. The CCA 
served as the foundation for identifying Ethiopia’s 
most pressing development gaps and opportunities, 
ensuring that the new Cooperation Framework is both 
responsive to the country’s needs and aligned with its 
long-term vision.
In addition to the CCA, the findings of the recently 
completed evaluation of the 2020–2025 UNSDCF 
provided critical insights that shaped the new 
Framework. The evaluation highlighted key 
achievements, challenges, and lessons learned, 
offering a valuable perspective on how the UN 
system can better leverage its comparative 
advantage to accelerate progress. Together, the 
CCA and the evaluation findings informed the 
prioritization process, ensuring that the new 
Cooperation Framework builds on past successes 
while addressing identified gaps.
Insights from the 2020–2025 UNSDCF 
Evaluation
The evaluation of the 2020–2025 UNSDCF 
underscored the relevance and adaptability of the 
previous Framework, which was well-aligned with 
Ethiopia’s national priorities, including the TYDP, 
and global commitments such as the SDGs. It also 
highlighted areas for improvement, such as addressing 
funding shortfalls, enhancing data availability, and 
strengthening coordination mechanisms. Key findings 
include:
Relevance and Adaptability: The 
UNSDCF demonstrated strong alignment 
with Ethiopia’s development priorities 
and responsiveness to emerging 
challenges, such as COVID-19, conflict, 
and climate shocks. This adaptability 
will remain a cornerstone of the new 
Cooperation Framework, ensuring it can 
respond effectively to future challenges.
Coherence and Coordination: While 
the previous Framework strengthened 
UN system coherence, challenges such 
as siloed mandates and underutilized 
coordination structures limited its full 
potential. The new Framework will 
prioritize integrated programming 
and enhanced coordination to foster 
synergies and maximize impact.
Effectiveness and Impact Orientation: 
Despite notable achievements in 
areas such as economic resilience, 
peacebuilding, and support for 
vulnerable groups, the evaluation 
highlighted the need for stronger 
monitoring systems and improved 
data availability. The new Framework 
will address these gaps by investing 
in robust data systems and evidencebased decision-making.
Efficiency: The catalytic role of the 
Resident Coordinator’s Office was 
recognized, but resource constraints 
and high transaction costs hindered 
efficiency. The new Framework will 
advocate for streamlined processes 
and adequate resourcing to enhance 
operational efficiency.
Sustainability: Efforts to promote 
national ownership and capacitybuilding were acknowledged as critical 
to sustainability. However, political 
instability, funding gaps, and fragmented 
interventions posed risks to long-term 
gains. The new Cooperation Framework 
will emphasize resilience-building, 
sustainable financing, and integrated 
approaches to ensure lasting impact.
These findings have been instrumental in shaping the 
strategic priorities of the 2025–2030 Cooperation 
Framework, ensuring that lessons learned from 
the previous cycle are fully integrated into the new 
approach.20 UNSDCF ETHIOPIA 2025-2030 UNSDCF ETHIOPIA 2025-2030 21
A Consultative and Inclusive Process
The consultative process for the new Cooperation 
Framework ensured inclusivity, transparency, and 
alignment with Ethiopia’s national development 
priorities, particularly its TYDP. The TYDP emphasizes 
inclusive economic growth, structural transformation, 
investments in social services, environmental 
sustainability, and gender equality. Through 
multi-stakeholder workshops, bilateral discussions, 
and thematic consultations, the process identified 
Ethiopia’s most pressing development gaps and 
challenges, as well as opportunities to achieve 
transformative results.
Special attention was given to incorporating the 
perspectives of vulnerable groups, including women, 
children, persons with disabilities, and communities 
affected by conflict and climate change. This 
inclusive approach ensures that the new Cooperation 
Framework not only addresses systemic challenges 
but also promotes equity and leaves no one behind.
From Evidence to Action
By combining the comprehensive insights of the 
CCA with the lessons learned from the 2020–
2025 UNSDCF evaluation, the new Cooperation 
Framework is designed to address Ethiopia’s evolving 
development needs. It builds on the successes of the 
previous cycle while introducing targeted measures 
to overcome identified challenges, such as improving 
data systems, enhancing coordination, and ensuring 
sustainable financing. This evidence-based and 
inclusive approach positions the UN system to deliver 
transformative results and accelerate progress 
toward the SDGs in Ethiopia.

and Strategic Priorities
The vision for the UNDS in Ethiopia reflects the 
country’s aspirations for sustainable development and 
the UN’s commitment to supporting transformative 
change. It is rooted in Ethiopia’s development context, 
the priorities outlined in its TYDP, and the global 
ambition of the 2030 Agenda. This vision seeks to 
address Ethiopia’s most pressing challenges while 
leveraging opportunities to achieve inclusive and 
sustainable development.
The overarching vision for the UNDS in Ethiopia is:
An equitable, peaceful, and prosperous Ethiopia, driven 
by self-reliance and resilience, where no one is left 
behind, and sustainable development is achieved for 
all by 2030.
To achieve this vision, five transformative results were 
identified in consultation with GoE:
1. End humanitarian dependency for the 
most vulnerable by fostering resilience 
through robust systems at all levels. 
2. Build sustainable food systems, 
value chains, and livelihoods to promote 
self-reliance.
3. Create three million jobs, with a focus 
on opportunities for youth and women 
to drive inclusive economic growth.
4. Digitize and modernize all aspects 
of development programming and 
service delivery to enhance efficiency, 
innovation, and impact.
5. Uphold shared values by leaving no 
one behind, ensuring targeted support 
for women, girls, children, persons with 
disabilities, and other vulnerable groups.
To deliver on these transformative results, 
five  interrelated strategic priorities were identified 
for the Cooperation Framework. These priorities 
address Ethiopia’s most critical development gaps 
while leveraging opportunities to accelerate progress 
across the SDGs. They also reflect areas where the 
UN’s expertise, mandate, and comparative advantage 
can have the greatest impact:
Peace and Governance: Strengthening 
institutions, fostering social cohesion, 
advancing human rights, and supporting 
the transitional justice process are 
essential foundations for sustainable 
development. Without peace, effective 
governance, and accountability, 
progress in other areas remains fragile 
and difficult to sustain.
Economy, Food Security, and Energy: 
Structural economic transformation—
including the modernization and 
optimization of agriculture, the 
development of sustainable food 
systems, and investments in renewable 
energy—is essential for improving 
livelihoods, reducing poverty, and 
enhancing food self-reliance.
Social Development: Building human 
capital through improved access to 
quality education, healthcare, social 
protection, and other basic social 
services is critical to ensuring equitable 
opportunities, particularly for vulnerable 
groups.
Environmental Sustainability, Resilience, 
and Preparedness: Addressing Ethiopia’s 
vulnerability to climate change through 
climate adaptation, disaster risk reduction, 
sustainable urban management and 
sustainable natural resource management 
is necessary to safeguard development 
gains and build resilience.
Gender Equality and Empowerment 
of Women and Young People: As a 
cross-cutting priority, gender equality 
underpins progress in all other areas. 
Addressing systemic inequalities and 
empowering women and girls ensures 
their full participation in development 
and governance processes, while driving 
broader social and economic benefits.
The selected priorities were chosen based on 
their potential to address Ethiopia’s most pressing 
challenges while creating a multiplier effect across 
the SDGs. For example, investments in peace and 
governance are essential for creating an enabling 
environment for sustainable development, fostering 
stability, and ensuring the protection of human rights. 
Economic transformation through investments 
in agriculture, energy, and industry can drive job 
creation, reduce poverty, and enhance the resilience 
of the food system. Social development is critical for 
building human capital and ensuring equitable access 
to opportunities, particularly for vulnerable groups. 
Environmental sustainability is necessary to mitigate 
the impacts of climate change, protect livelihoods, 
and ensure long-term development gains. Gender 
equality is a catalyst for progress across all sectors, 
as empowering women and girls leads to broader 
social and economic benefits.
The UN’s comparative advantage lies in its ability 
to address complex, multidimensional challenges, 
its normative role in advancing human rights and 
gender equality, and its capacity to convene diverse 
stakeholders. These strengths position the UN to 
deliver transformative results in Ethiopia, particularly 
in areas requiring impartiality, technical expertise, 
and engagement on sensitive issues such as 
peacebuilding, migration, and human rights.
The selected priorities align closely with Ethiopia’s 
TYDP and the 2030 Agenda, ensuring coherence 
between national and global development goals. By 
focusing on these areas, the Cooperation Framework 
addresses Ethiopia’s most critical challenges while 
leveraging opportunities to accelerate progress

2.2 Theory of Change for the 
Cooperation Framework Priorities
The Theory of Change for the UNSDCF is designed to 
address Ethiopia’s complex development challenges 
while fostering resilience, self-reliance, and inclusive 
growth. It emphasizes the need to tackle root 
causes of inequality, vulnerability, and exclusion, 
while leveraging Ethiopia’s strong commitment to 
the SDGs, its TYDP, and the Africa Agenda 2063. 
By addressing these challenges and capitalizing 
on opportunities, the UNSDCF aims to accelerate 
Ethiopia’s progress toward achieving its vision of an 
equitable, peaceful, and prosperous Ethiopia, driven 
by self-reliance and resilience, where no one is left 
behind, and sustainable development is achieved for 
all by 2030.
The Theory of Change focuses on five interrelated 
outcomes that address Ethiopia’s development gaps 
and create a multiplier effect across the SDGs:
Peace and Governance: Ensuring that 
all people in Ethiopia, particularly those 
left behind, live in a peaceful, just, and 
democratic society that upholds the rule 
of law, accountability, and human rights. 
Peace and governance are foundational 
for sustainable development and 
conflict prevention, as they create an 
enabling environment for progress in 
all other areas. Strengthening inclusive 
governance, fostering meaningful 
participation in decision-making 
processes, promoting social cohesion, 
and building accountable institutions are 
critical to achieving sustainable peace 
and development. The UN’s impartiality 
and expertise in these areas position it 
to support Ethiopia in advancing these 
priorities.
Inclusive Economic Development: 
Ensuring that all people in Ethiopia, 
particularly those left behind, benefit 
from resilient and sustainable economic 
growth that prioritizes decent job 
opportunities, access to nutritious food, 
and affordable green energy. Structural 
economic transformation—including 
the modernization and optimization 
of agriculture, industry, and energy 
sectors, as well as the promotion of 
small and medium enterprises (SMEs) 
and the socioeconomic empowerment 
of women and youth—is essential 
for improving livelihoods, creating 
jobs, and achieving food self-reliance. 
Supporting inclusive and sustainable 
food systems, value chain development, 
entrepreneurship, skills development, 
and renewable energy aligns with 
Ethiopia’s goals of building a resilient 
green economy and reducing aid 
dependency. The UNSDCF will promote 
policy coherence and mechanisms to 
manage trade-offs between industrial 
growth and environmental sustainability, 
ensuring that economic transformation 
does not compromise Ethiopia’s natural 
resources or climate resilience.
Social Development: Ensuring that all 
people in Ethiopia, particularly those 
left behind, have access to quality 
social services and protection. Social 
development is critical for building 
human capital and ensuring equitable 
access to opportunities. Improving 
access to quality education, healthcare, 
and social protection is essential for 
addressing the needs of vulnerable 
populations, including women, children, 
adolescent and young people, persons 
with disabilities, IDPs, and refugees. The 
UN’s expertise in these areas enables 
it to support Ethiopia in strengthening 
systems and services that promote 
equity and inclusion.
Environmental Sustainability and 
Resilience: Strengthening environmental 
sustainability and resilience to ensure that 
all people in Ethiopia, particularly those 
left behind, are protected from climateinduced disasters and environmental 
crises. Ethiopia’s vulnerability to climate 
change highlights the need for climate 
adaptation, disaster risk reduction, 
resilient cities and human settlements, and 
sustainable natural resource management 
to safeguard development gains and build 
resilience. The UNCT will emphasize 
the synergies between environmental 
sustainability and other SDGs, such as 
poverty reduction, food security, and 
health, while addressing potential tradeoffs through integrated planning and 
policy advice. Supporting these efforts 
is critical to promoting self-reliance and 
ensuring long-term sustainability.
Gender Equality and Empowerment of 
Women and Young People: Ensuring 
that all women and young people, 
particularly adolescent girls and 
those left behind, enjoy equitable 
opportunities and are empowered 
to participate fully in all aspects of 
society. Gender equality and the 
empowerment of women and young 
people are cross-cutting priorities that 
drive progress across all development 
areas. Addressing structural barriers, 
promoting women’s agency and 
leadership, and ensuring equitable 
access to opportunities are essential 
for achieving sustainable development 
and fostering inclusive growth.
To achieve these outcomes, the UNSDCF identifies 
a set of outputs that represent critical pathways 
to change. These include strengthening peace 
and conflict resolution mechanisms, promoting 
democratic governance and the rule of law, 
supporting economic governance and job creation, 
improving access to energy, enhancing health 
and education services, building disaster risk 
management (DRM) systems, advancing climate 
adaptation, and promoting gender equality. To 
ensure coherence and maximize impact, the 
framework will advance integrated approaches 
to SDG implementation, leveraging synergies 
between goals while addressing trade-offs through 
evidence-based analysis, stakeholder engagement, 
and adaptive policy-making. The outputs are 
supported by cross-cutting strategies such as policy 
dialogue and advocacy, capacity building, systems 
strengthening, behaviour change communication, 
monitoring and evaluation, and the utilization of data 
and digital solutions.
The Theory of Change recognizes that achieving 
these outcomes requires a holistic, integrated, 
and inclusive approach. Equity, equality, inclusion, 
compliance with human rights, and sustainability are 
embedded as cross-cutting principles throughout 
the UNSDCF, ensuring that no one is left behind. 
Development efforts are designed to be inclusive, 
transformational, catalytic, equitable, nationallyowned and environmentally sustainable. The 
framework also emphasizes agility, adaptive 
approaches, accountability, and results-oriented 
implementation, with robust monitoring and 
evaluation mechanisms to track progress, foster 
learning, and respond effectively to emerging 
opportunities and challenges.
Localization is central to the framework, ensuring 
that development efforts are rooted in local contexts, 
driven by local actors, and responsive to the needs 
of communities. In this regard, volunteerism is 
recognized as a valuable means of fostering 
community engagement, strengthening local 
ownership, and supporting the implementation of the 
2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.
By addressing systemic barriers, promoting 
synergies, and managing trade-offs between SDGs, 
the UNSDCF creates the conditions necessary for 
achieving Ethiopia’s vision of an equitable, peaceful,

2.3 United Nations Comparative 
Advantage 
The UNDS in Ethiopia brings a unique and unparalleled 
comparative advantage to the implementation of 
the UNSDCF. Ethiopia hosts the largest UNCT in 
the world, comprising 25 agencies with diverse 
and complementary mandates, expertise, and 
comparative advantages. This presence is both 
symbolically and materially significant, as Ethiopia is 
one of the first African founding Member States of the 
United Nations. The country is also home to the United 
Nations Economic Commission for Africa (UNECA), 
the United Nations Office to the African Union (AU), 
and the Office of the Special Envoy of the SecretaryGeneral for the Horn of Africa, further enhancing 
the UN’s ability to support Ethiopia’s development 
priorities and regional leadership.
The UN’s comparative advantage in Ethiopia is 
rooted in its long-standing relationship of trust with 
the Government and people of Ethiopia, built over 
nearly 50 years of presence and collaboration through 
successes and crises. The UN is widely recognized 
as an impartial partner, representing global values 
and principles rather than individual national 
agendas. Its normative role and tripartite mandate 
across sustainable development, human rights, and 
peacebuilding uniquely position the UN to address 
Ethiopia’s most pressing challenges. The UN’s ability 
to engage on sensitive and complex issues—such 
as electoral support, migration, care of refugees, 
transitional justice, and human rights—sets it apart 
from other development partners. This is further 
reinforced by its track record of delivering results 
in these areas, combining technical expertise with 
robust monitoring and accountability mechanisms.
The UN’s convening power is a defining feature 
of its role in Ethiopia. It brings together diverse 
stakeholders—including the Government, civil 
society, development partners, and the private 
sector—to foster dialogue, build consensus, and 
mobilize resources for transformative change. This 
convening role is complemented by the UN’s ability to 
provide integrated solutions that address Ethiopia’s 
development challenges holistically, leveraging its 
global experience and technical expertise across 
multiple sectors. In doing so, the UN works in synergy 
with other development partners, such as international 
financial institutions (IFIs), by complementing their 
large-scale financing and technical expertise with 
its focus on inclusive policy development, capacity 
building, and ensuring alignment with global norms 
and principles. This collaborative approach ensures 
that development efforts are impactful, sustainable, 
and aligned with Ethiopia’s priorities.
The UN’s large and extensive field presence enables 
it to operate at national, regional, and local levels, 
ensuring that its support reaches the most vulnerable 
populations and aligns with Ethiopia’s development 
priorities. By combining its convening power, 
technical expertise, and monitoring capabilities, 
the UN is uniquely positioned to support Ethiopia in 
achieving its vision of becoming an African Beacon of 
Prosperity. Its impartiality, depth of experience, field 
presence and ability to address multidimensional 
challenges ensure that the UN remains a trusted and 
complementary partner in Ethiopia’s journey toward 
sustainable development, peace, and prosperity.

Strategic Priority 1: Peace and Governance
Outcome 1: All people in Ethiopia, particularly those 
left behind, live in a peaceful, just, and democratic 
society that upholds the rule of law, accountability, 
and human rights.
Pathways to Change
Achieving sustainable peace, good governance, 
and respect for human rights in Ethiopia requires 
addressing the root causes of conflict, strengthening 
governance systems, and empowering citizens—
particularly those left behind—to claim their rights and 
meaningfully participate in governance processes. 
Progress toward this outcome depends on the 
adoption and implementation of laws, policies, and 
regulatory frameworks that align with international 
standards; the strengthening of institutional 
capacities to ensure accountability, transparency, and 
equitable service delivery; and the empowerment of 
citizens to engage in governance processes.
If Ethiopia adopts and implements laws, policies, and 
regulatory frameworks that align with international 
standards, then the country will establish a strong 
legal foundation for peace, justice, and human 
rights, ensuring accountability and transparency in 
governance. If institutional capacities are strengthened 
to deliver equitable and transparent services, prevent 
conflict, and promote accountability, then trust in 
governance systems will increase, fostering social 
cohesion and reducing the risk of conflict. If citizens, 
particularly vulnerable groups, are empowered to 
engage in governance processes and claim their 
rights, then governance systems will become more 
inclusive, participatory, and responsive to the needs 
of all people. If mechanisms for transitional justice, 
national dialogue, and reconciliation are implemented 
effectively, then Ethiopia will address the root causes 
of conflict, promote healing, and build a foundation 
for lasting peace.
This is because strengthened legal and institutional 
frameworks, improved knowledge and capacities, and 
inclusive governance mechanisms will ensure that 
all people, particularly those left behind, can live with 
dignity and justice. These changes will foster trust and 
social cohesion, creating a peaceful and democratic 
environment that supports inclusive, self-reliant, and 
sustainable development.
UN Development Support and Partnerships to 
Achieve the Outcome
The UN’s contributions to this outcome are structured 
around five key areas of focus, each addressing critical 
pathways to achieving peace, good governance, and 
human rights in Ethiopia.
The first area of focus is strengthening institutions, 
systems, and mechanisms to promote peace, 
prevent conflict, and implement inclusive postconflict rehabilitation efforts. The UN will support 
the implementation of peace agreements, including 
provisions related to transitional justice and 
Disarmament, Demobilization, and Reintegration 
(DDR) programs as part of broader peacebuilding 
efforts and the national dialogue. As part of these 
efforts, the UN will work to strengthen reconciliation 
and social cohesion by supporting inclusive dialogue. 
Beyond this, the UN will advocate for and support the 
implementation of the Youth, Peace, and Security 
and Women, Peace, and Security UN resolutions, 
promoting the participation of women and youth in 
conflict prevention, peacebuilding, and reconciliation 
processes. The UN will also work to build the capacity 
of government agencies responsible for conflict 
prevention and management, while empowering civil 
society organizations (CSOs), media, academia, and 
youth and women’s groups to act as agents of peace.
The second area of focus is strengthening democratic 
institutions and governance structures to ensure 
good governance, electoral integrity, and institutional 
accountability. The UN will invest in building the 
capacity of governance bodies and democratic 
institutions, including parliament and the National 
Electoral Board of Ethiopia, to promote democratic 
practices and ensure transparency. Support will 
include technical assistance for anti-corruption 
initiatives, improved budget allocation processes, and 
preparations for upcoming elections. These efforts 
aim to foster trust, inclusivity, and transparency in 
governance systems.
The third area of focus is on strengthening legal, 
policy, regulatory, and accountability frameworks to 
ensure equitable access to justice and uphold the 
rule of law. The UN will support the development 
of inclusive and accountable justice systems and 
advocate for reforms to enhance the rule of law. 
Efforts will prioritize improving access to justice for 
vulnerable groups, including women and children, 
and expanding legal aid services. Additionally, the 
UN will advocate for the ratification of outstanding 
international human rights treaties and support the 
implementation of transitional justice measures—
such as justice, reparations, and truth-seeking—in line 
with international standards.
The fourth area of focus is enhancing the capacities 
of institutions, CSOs, and citizens to promote and 
protect human rights, including through strengthened 
civic engagement and expanded civic space. The UN 
will empower rights holders, including women, youth, 
victims’ associations and vulnerable groups, to access 
and exercise their rights. It will also strengthen the 
capacity of CSOs, academia, and media to promote 
civic space, democracy, and media freedoms. 
Additionally, the UN will enhance the capacity of 
the Ethiopian Human Rights Commission (EHRC) to 
monitor and report human rights violations, ensuring 
accountability and protection for all.
The fifth area of focus is enhancing national and 
regional capacities for the production, analysis, 
and utilization of high-quality data. This includes 
strengthening the capacity of the national statistical 
office, improving administrative data systems, 
and integrating alternative data sources, such as 
citizen-generated data. By improving the availability 
and accessibility of disaggregated data, the UN 
will support evidence-based policymaking and 
programming that addresses the needs of those left 
behind.
UNCT Configuration
The UN entities supporting this outcome include ILO, 
IOM, OCHA, OHCHR, UNDP, UNFPA, UNHCR, UNICEF, 
UNODC, UN Women, and WHO. Together, these 
entities bring a wealth of expertise in governance, 
peacebuilding, human rights, and data systems. Their 
collective capacities will be leveraged to provide 
technical assistance, advocacy, and capacity-building 
support to national and sub-national stakeholders, 
ensuring a coordinated and impactful approach to 
achieving this outcome.
Building on field-level collaboration, UN entities will 
enhance coordination through referral-based support, 
where each agency contributes according to its 
mandate and comparative advantage. This approach 
ensures that assistance reaches those in need 
more efficiently, avoids duplication, and strengthens 
national efforts.

and macroeconomic management, improving access 
to finance, markets, and technology, promoting 
sustainable livelihoods, and fostering the adoption of 
climate-smart agricultural practices and renewable 
energy technologies for productive uses.
If Ethiopia strengthens its economic governance, 
institutional capacity, social dialogue, and 
macroeconomic management; if policies, systems, 
and institutional capacities are enhanced and are 
inclusive of relevant stakeholders, including social 
partners, to create decent and inclusive jobs and 
improve access to finance and technology; if inputs 
(e.g., seeds, technologies, implements, mechanization, 
and extension services), technologies, and practices 
for producing and utilizing nutrient-dense food are 
widely adopted to build an inclusive and resilient food 
system; and if financing for energy investment, private 
sector engagement, and private sector development 
are scaled up, then all people in Ethiopia, particularly 
those left behind, will participate in and benefit 
from inclusive, resilient, and sustainable economic 
transformation.
This is because a transformed economy with 
improved governance, sustainable and diversified 
food systems, community-based nutrition programs, 
and better access to affordable and clean energy 
will create decent and inclusive jobs, improve the 
ease of doing business, enhance self-reliance, and 
reduce poverty and inequalities. These changes will 
ensure that Ethiopia’s economic growth is inclusive, 
sustainable, and aligned with the needs of its most 
vulnerable populations.
UN Development Support and Partnerships to 
Achieve the Outcome
The UN’s contributions to this outcome are structured 
around four key areas of focus, each addressing 
critical pathways to achieving inclusive economic 
development, resilient food systems, and access to 
clean energy in Ethiopia.
The first area of focus is strengthening economic 
governance and institutional capacity. The UN will 
strengthen the capacity of state and non-state 
institutions engaged in policy analysis, design, and 
implementation. This includes providing evidencebased policy advice, promoting social dialogue, 
and encouraging the active involvement of social 
partners. The UN will also support the testing of 
new policy and regulatory measures through a 
regulatory sandbox system. Efforts will include 
enhancing statistical systems to collect, analyze, 
disaggregate, and disseminate data for tracking 
progress toward the SDGs. Additionally, the UN will 
support institutional infrastructure at federal and 
sub-regional levels to adapt and implement policies 
and frameworks using a whole-of-government and 
whole-of-society approach, ensuring their effective 
execution. Revitalizing local economies in fragile and 
post-conflict settings will also be prioritized through 
community-led recovery, inclusive market access, and 
small-scale enterprise support. Advocacy efforts will 
focus on securing sufficient resources for capacity 
development programs, including civil service 
reform, and strengthening public and private sector 
accountability for delivering on national, regional, and 
international commitments.
The second area of focus is creating decent and 
inclusive jobs. The UN will advocate for increased 
investments in high-growth sectors, including green 
jobs in renewable energy, sustainable agriculture, 
community-based nutrition, and environmental 
conservation. Support will be provided to SMEs through 
entrepreneurship training, youth-based start-ups, 
business management education, skills development, 
financial literacy programs, and access to funding and 
local, regional, and international markets, particularly 
in the context of the AfCFTA. The UN will also promote 
youth entrepreneurship by offering incentives for 
youth to engage not only in the rural economy but 
also in technology-driven, growth-oriented, and 
innovative start-ups. Strengthening vocational 
programs and fostering public-private partnerships to 
align education, training, and skills development with 
industry needs will also be prioritized. Employment 
services will be enhanced through skills training, 
continued education, and volunteerism deployments 
to improve access to decent jobs. Furthermore, the 
UN will drive the structural transformation of the 
Ethiopian economy, aiming to reduce rural poverty 
and create a better environment for increased 
investment in agro-food and allied sectors. This will 
create market opportunities for farmers and promote 
local food processing by adding value to agricultural 
outputs with the involvement of the private sector, 
strengthening the link between smallholder farmers 
and industry. Additionally, the UN will work with 
government institutions to improve employment 
services, including labor market information systems, 
oversight mechanisms for financial institutions, and 
labor migration and remittance systems.
The third area of focus is building inclusive and 
resilient food systems. The UN will promote the 
dissemination and adoption of climate-smart and 
sustainable agricultural technologies, introduce 
innovative systems to mitigate and manage risks 
such as insurance and risk finance, and enable the 
production and utilization of diversified and nutrientdense food. Efforts will focus on improving access to 
quality and affordable inputs, increasing investments 
in irrigation and ecosystem restoration, urban 
agriculture and reducing post-harvest losses. The 
UN will enhance the enabling environment for private 
sector capital investment in the agrifood system 
to strengthen market linkages among food system 
actors, mainly smallholder farmers and industry. 
The UN will also strengthen agricultural institutions, 
including extension and research systems, and 
enhance the policy environment to attract private 
sector engagement in agriculture and food systems. 
Coordination among stakeholders will be improved 
through investment forums, strengthened market 
information systems, and enhanced food safety and 
quality standards infrastructure.
The fourth area of focus is enhancing access to 
affordable and clean energy. The UN will promote 
renewable energy concepts by prototyping business 
models and technologies with private sector 
participation. Efforts will include promoting standalone solar and clean cooking technologies, supporting 
biogas and solar energy demonstration projects, 
and advancing mini-grid pilot implementations. 
The UN will also advocate for sustainable financial 
mechanisms, including de-risking investments in 
renewable energy technologies, and strengthen 
regulatory and legal frameworks to support renewable 
energy adoption. Public awareness campaigns will 
be conducted to promote the benefits of renewable 
energy technologies, particularly in rural areas and 
conflict-affected regions.

transformation, renewable energy, and livelihoods

programs. Their collective capacities will be leveraged 
to provide technical assistance, advocacy, and 
capacity-building support to national and sub-national 
stakeholders, ensuring a coordinated and impactful 
approach to achieving this outcome.

Strategic Priority 3: Social services and 
protection
Outcome 3: All people in Ethiopia more specifically

Pathways to Change
Achieving equitable access to quality social services 
and protection in Ethiopia requires addressing 
systemic bottlenecks and barriers in health, 
education, water, sanitation, and social protection 
systems. Progress toward this outcome depends on 
strengthening national and sub-national capacities 
to deliver inclusive, gender-responsive, and climateresilient services, improving governance and financing 
mechanisms, and empowering communities to 
access and utilize these services.
If national health care systems are strengthened to 
ensure equitable access to integrated, resilient, and 
shock-responsive primary health care services; if the 
education system is equipped to provide inclusive 
and equitable learning opportunities for out-ofschool and hard-to-reach children, adolescents and 
young people; if more people and families in rural 
and urban areas have access to basic, inclusive, 
and climate-resilient water, sanitation, and hygiene 
(WASH) services; and if social protection systems 
are enhanced to provide gender-responsive, disabilityinclusive, climate-resilient, and shock-responsive 
services to all, including vulnerable populations, then 
all people in Ethiopia, particularly those left behind, 
will have access to equitable, quality social services 
and protection.
This is because strengthening these systems and 
services will ensure that vulnerable populations, 
including children, youth, women, people with 
disabilities, workers in the informal sector, older 
persons, and those in hard-to-reach areas, can access 
the resources they need to live with dignity, resilience, 
and self-reliance. These changes will contribute 
to Ethiopia’s human capital development, create a 
foundation for sustainable and inclusive growth, 
enhance social cohesion, and prevent conflict.
UN Development Support and Partnerships to 
Achieve the Outcome
The UN’s contributions to this outcome are structured 
around four key areas of focus, each addressing 
critical pathways to achieving equitable access to 
quality social services and protection in Ethiopia.
The first area of focus is strengthening national health 
care system capacities to ensure equitable access to 
integrated, resilient, and shock-responsive primary 
health care services. The UN will work to improve 
policies and governance, with a focus on vulnerable 
groups and gender mainstreaming, and advocate 
for increased resources and equitable budgeting for 
health services. Efforts will include strengthening 
Universal Health Coverage through innovative and 
sustainable health financing mechanisms, including 
community-based health insurance (CBHI), improving 
access to comprehensive sexual, reproductive, 
maternal, newborn, child, and adolescent health 
services, and addressing gender-based violence 
(GBV) and HIV/AIDS prevention and treatment with 
particular attention to young girls as part of broader 
sexual and reproductive health initiatives. Recognizing 
the heightened vulnerabilities of young women and 
girls - particularly in the context of crises such as 
pandemics and conflict - the UN will support gendersensitive strategies that address the unique barriers 
faced by female youth, including disrupted access 
to health and social services and harmful practices. 
The UN will also enhance health workforce systems 
at both facility and community levels, supply chains, 
and information systems, leveraging digital solutions 
and volunteerism to improve service delivery and 
evidence generation. Additionally, the UN will support 
health emergency preparedness, response, and 
recovery, while fostering partnerships and community 
engagement to strengthen health programming.
The second area focuses on strengthening the 
national education system to increase access 
to inclusive, equitable, and quality learning 
opportunities for out-of-school and hard-to-reach 
children and adolescents. The UN will advocate for 
data-driven decision-making and policies that ensure 
equitable access to education, increased funding, 
improved teaching, and alignment with SDG 4 goals.
Efforts will include expanding the provision of 
Accelerated Education Programmes, improving 
and restoring educational infrastructure to enhance 
access for children with disabilities, expanding school 
feeding programs for vulnerable populations, investing 
in gender-responsive and student-centered teacher 
training, and providing inclusive learning materials 
and assessments. The UN will also collaborate with 
communities to create safe and inclusive learning 
environments, address harmful social norms, and 
expand TVET programs and other skills and training 
programs to equip youth with skills for successful 
transitions from learning to earning.
The third area emphasizes strengthening national 
and sub-national capacities to provide equitable 
access to basic, inclusive, and climate-resilient 
WASH services. The UN will strengthen government 
systems to deliver gender-responsive WASH 
services in both development and humanitarian 
contexts, develop resilient WASH infrastructure for 
communities facing recurrent natural disasters, and 
ensure equitable access to WASH services for rural, 
urban, and refugee populations. Efforts will also 
focus on integrating WASH and menstrual hygiene 
management (MHM) services in schools, health 
facilities, and other institutions, while promoting 
positive WASH behaviors through social behavior 
change campaigns.
The fourth area focuses on strengthening national 
and sub-national capacities to deliver genderresponsive, disability-inclusive, climate-resilient, and 
shock-responsive child protection, social protection, 
and social services to all. The UN will support 
early warning and disaster preparedness systems, 
leveraging digital tools and community engagement 
to enhance the timeliness and adequacy of social 
protection services. Efforts will include rolling 
out child protection case management systems, 
strengthening essential services for GBV survivors, 
and expanding and sustaining the social service 
workforce to provide holistic services to protect 
women and children. The UN will also advocate for 
increased spending in social sectors, promote a 
lifecycle approach to social protection programming, 
and support the development of disability-inclusive 
and gender-responsive policies and legislation on 
child social protection. Finally, the UN will promote 
social protection coverage for all workers and their 
families, including those in the informal sector, by 
supporting initiatives aimed at achieving SDG 1.3, 
ensuring that social protection systems, including 
floors, leave no one behind.

Outcome 4: All people in Ethiopia more specifically

Pathways to Change
Reducing Ethiopia’s vulnerability to climate-induced 
disasters and environmental crises requires 
monitoring and forecasting disasters, strengthening 
DRM systems, building the capacity of government and 
communities to adapt to and mitigate climate change 
variations, promoting sustainable natural resource 
management, and mobilizing climate financing. 
Progress toward this outcome depends on improving 
governance and institutional capacities, empowering 
communities to adopt climate-smart solutions, and 
integrating resilience-building measures into national 
and sub-national development plans.
If disaster risk management systems are strengthened 
at all levels; if government and community capacities 
to respond, adapt, and build resilience to climate 
extremes, environmental shocks, and climate change 
are enhanced; if sustainable management of natural 
resources and proper waste management, including 
circular economy approaches, is promoted; if 
urbanization and human settlements are managed 
sustainably; and if adequate climate financing is 
mobilized and utilized effectively, then all people in 
Ethiopia, particularly the most vulnerable—including 
children, women, displaced people, and those 
affected by extreme poverty—will enjoy protection 
and benefit from enhanced resilience, reduced risks 
of climate-induced disasters, and reduced impacts of 
environmental and ecosystem crises.
This is because improved disaster risk management 
systems, strengthened government and community 
capacities, and sustainable management of natural 
resources will enable Ethiopia to strengthen resilience 
to climate change, reduce vulnerabilities, and ensure 
inclusive and sustainable development. These 
changes will contribute to Ethiopia’s long-term lowemission and climate-resilient development strategy, 
creating a foundation for self-reliance and prosperity.
UN Development Support and Partnerships to 
Achieve the Outcome
The UN’s contributions to this outcome are structured 
around five key areas of focus, each addressing critical 
pathways to achieving environmental sustainability, 
resilience, and preparedness in Ethiopia.
The first area of focus is strengthening DRM systems 
and capacities at all levels. The UN will support the 
development and implementation of DRM strategies 
and policies, focusing on government coordination, 
legal enforcement, and localized climate forecasting. 
Efforts will include improving infrastructure, risk 
knowledge, disaster loss and damage tracking 
capabilities and technologies and tools for DRM, as 
well as enhancing multi-hazard early warning systems 
and integrating them with preventive measures. 
The UN will also promote the mainstreaming of 
DRM across all sectors and development plans, 
strengthen real-time monitoring for early warning and 
action, and enhance coordination and accountability 
among clusters and sectors in disaster management 
programming.
The second area focuses on strengthening the 
capacity of government, including in key social 
sectors, and communities to respond, adapt, and 
build resilience to climate change and environmental 
shocks. The UN will support the adaptation and 
implementation of climate-adaptive policies, 
practices, and green technologies, emphasizing the 
use of adequate technologies and data in decisionmaking processes. Efforts will include increasing 
community awareness of climate change mitigation 
and adaptation, promoting climate-smart agriculture, 
nature-based solutions, and climate-resilient 
development, mitigating the impact of climateinduced displacement and negative household coping 
mechanisms, and advocating for social safety nets to 
reinforce access to agricultural extension services. 
The UN will also enhance resource mobilization for 
environmental and resilience development financing, 
including from international funds such as the 
Loss and Damage Fund and the Adaptation Fund. 
Partnerships will be strengthened to identify new nontraditional development partners and promote risk 
financing mechanisms, such as crop and weatherindexed insurance.
The third area emphasizes enhancing sustainable 
natural resource management. The UN will 
strengthen the capacity of government and national 
and sub-national entities to implement policies 
and mechanisms for managing the environment 
and promoting ecosystem integrity. Efforts will 
include supporting the development of sustainable 
natural resource management systems, promoting 
conservation and sound management of land, forests, 
wildlife, water, ecosystems, chemicals, and waste, and 
facilitating access to financing mechanisms such as 
carbon financing, payments for ecosystem services, 
and circular economy approaches. The UN will also 
engage communities in natural resource and waste 
management, ensuring their active participation 
in conservation efforts and raising awareness 
of the impacts of improper waste and chemical 
management.
The fourth area focuses on strengthening the 
capacity of government and other stakeholders 
for the sustainable management of urbanization 
and human settlements. The UN will support 
spatial development planning, the implementation 
of integrated urban development plans, and the 
construction of climate- and environment-resilient 
infrastructure and risk-informed development. Efforts 
will include strengthening urban waste management 
systems, promoting sustainable consumption and 
production, and supporting the provision of adequate 
and affordable housing. The UN will also assist in 
planning and developing human settlements for IDPs 
and refugees, ensuring their safety and sustainability.
The fifth area focuses on improving access to 
environment and resilience-building finance to support 
Ethiopia’s long-term low-emission and climateresilient development strategy. The UN will leverage 
diversified and innovative financing mechanisms, 
including international cooperation and private sector 
financing, to mobilize resources for climate-resilient 
development programs. Efforts will also include 
building local capacity to develop, implement, and 
manage climate-resilient initiatives, ensuring that 
financing is effectively utilized to achieve sustainable 
outcomes.

adolescent girls in Ethiopia, particularly those left 
behind, enjoyed equitable opportunities and are 
empowered to participate fully in all aspects of 
society, leading to their full potential being realized.
Pathways to Change
Achieving gender equality and empowering women, 
girls, and youth in Ethiopia requires addressing 
systemic barriers, long-standing discriminatory social 
norms, and gender-based violence while promoting 
inclusive policies, institutional accountability, and 
equitable access to services and opportunities. 
Progress toward this outcome depends on 
strengthening mechanisms and capacities of 
communities and institutions to address gender 
inequalities, increasing the equal representation and 
meaningful participation of women, including young 
women and youth, in decision-making processes, and 
ensuring that policies and financing frameworks are in 
place to promote gender equality and empowerment 
of women and youth.
If mechanisms and capacities of communities 
and institutions are strengthened to address 
discriminatory gender and social norms and laws and 
to prevent and respond to all forms of gender-based 
violence, including sexual exploitation and abuse 
in the workplace and elsewhere; if the participation 
and representation of women, girls, youth, and 
vulnerable groups in multi-sectoral decision-making 
processes are increased; and if policies, institutional 
accountability, and financing frameworks are 
strengthened to promote gender equality and the 
empowerment of women, girls, and youth, then all 
women and young people, including adolescent girls, 
particularly those left behind, will enjoy equitable 
opportunities and be empowered to participate fully 
in all aspects of society.
This is because women, girls, and youth will have 
decision-making power not only to influence favourable 
policies but also legislative frameworks, strategies, 
and systems. Gender- and youth-specific needs will 
be addressed in governance and service delivery, and 
barriers to economic autonomy and dignified lives 
will be removed. These changes will contribute to an 
equitable and prosperous society where no one is 
left behind, and sustainable development is achieved 
by all.
UN Development Support and Partnerships to 
Achieve the Outcome
The UN’s contributions to this outcome are structured 
around three key areas of focus, each addressing 
critical pathways to achieving gender equality and the 
empowerment of women and youth in Ethiopia.
The first area of focus is strengthening mechanisms 
and capacities of communities and institutions to 
address discriminatory gender and social norms 
and to prevent and respond to all forms of genderbased violence, including violence against women 
in elections/politics and sexual exploitation and 
abuse in the workplace and elsewhere. At the 
community level, the UN will empower individuals 
and communities to access information, goods, 
and services, and to challenge harmful practices 
such as limiting women’s access to and control over 
strategic resources, including education, leadership 
and decision-making positions, land ownership, and 
economic opportunities. Community volunteerism 
initiatives will be leveraged to support these efforts, 
particularly in raising awareness and fostering local 
leadership to challenge harmful norms and practices. 
At the institutional level, the UN will advocate for 
policy and legal reforms to eliminate discriminatory 
practices and strengthen the capacity of institutions 
and systems to provide justice, reproductive health, 
and violence prevention and response services. By 
addressing these barriers, the UN will help to increase 
women’s participation in the labor market, promote 
the protection of their rights, including labor rights, 
reduce gender inequalities, and enable women and 
girls to fulfill their potential.
The second areafocuses on increasing the meaningful 
participation and representation of women, youth, 
and vulnerable groups, including adolescent girls, in 
multi-sectoral decision-making processes, notably 
in conflict-affected settings. The UN will strengthen 
systems to improve human capacity-building 
services, including literacy initiatives and access to 
health and education services, to enhance women’s 
and girls’ education opportunities and outcomes. 
Leadership development programs and mentorship 
opportunities will be promoted to prepare women 
and youth for decision-making roles, while multistakeholder dialogues and awareness campaigns will 
advocate for their participation in public, economic 
and political life.
The third area emphasizes strengthening policies, 
institutional accountability, and financing frameworks 
to promote gender equality and the empowerment 
of women and youth. The UN will advocate for 
Ethiopia’s legal and policy frameworks to uphold 
and mainstream gender equality and women’s and 
young people’s empowerment, while supporting 
coordination and accountability mechanisms at 
national and sub-national levels. Efforts will include 
enhancing the capacity of government ministries 
and the three branches of government to create 
an enabling environment for gender-responsive 
and youth-inclusive outcomes, including genderresponsive and youth-focused budgeting, and 
strengthening national and regional capacities to 
produce, analyze, and utilize high-quality data on 
gender equality and youth engagement.
UNCT Configuration
The UN entities supporting this outcome include 
FAO, IFAD, ILO, IOM, OHCHR, UNDP, UNESCO, UNFPA, 
UNICEF, UN Women, and WFP. Together, these 
entities bring a wealth of expertise in gender equality, 
women’s empowerment, youth engagement, and 
social protection. Their collective capacities will be 
leveraged to provide technical assistance, advocacy, 
and capacity-building support to national and subnational stakeholders, ensuring a coordinated and 
impactful approach to achieving this outcome.
This strategic priority will act as a wrap-around that 
will help to shape and inform all UN interventions, 
ensuring gender and social inclusion are fully 
integrated at all levels of the UNSDCF.

2.5 Enablers for Achieving the 
Cooperation Framework Outcomes 
The successful implementation of the Cooperation 
Framework relies on several cross-cutting enablers 
that underpin all strategic priorities and outcomes. 
These enablers ensure that interventions are inclusive, 
sustainable, and aligned with Ethiopia’s development 
aspirations and global commitments, including the 
2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the 
Africa Agenda 2063. The key enablers are outlined 
below.
2.5.1 Leave No One Behind
The principle of Leave No One Behind (LNOB) is at 
the heart of the Cooperation Framework, ensuring 
that the most vulnerable populations are prioritized 
in all interventions. LNOB is not only a guiding 
principle but also a commitment to addressing 
systemic barriers and inequalities that perpetuate 
exclusion. The Cooperation Framework focuses 
on populations disproportionately affected by 
crises, including displaced persons, women, youth, 
persons with disabilities, and those living in extreme 
poverty. Special attention is given to groups facing 
intersecting vulnerabilities, such as female-headed 
households, children in conflict-affected areas, and 
rural populations with limited access to services.
To operationalize LNOB, the UN will work to 
dismantle structural inequalities by promoting 
inclusive governance, equitable access to services, 
and targeted support for vulnerable groups. This 
includes advocating for policy and legal reforms, 
strengthening institutional accountability, and 
addressing discriminatory social norms that 
perpetuate exclusion. Vulnerable groups will be 
empowered to meaningfully participate in decisionmaking processes, governance, and development 
initiatives, ensuring their voices are heard and their 
needs are addressed. The UN will also strengthen 
data systems to collect and analyze disaggregated 
data, enabling evidence-based policymaking and 
programming that leaves no one behind. The use of 
citizen-generated data and participatory monitoring 
mechanisms will further ensure that interventions 
are inclusive and responsive to the needs of the 
most vulnerable.
By addressing the root causes of exclusion and 
promoting equitable access to opportunities and 
services, the Cooperation Framework ensures that no 
one is left behind in Ethiopia’s development journey. 
This commitment is embedded across all strategic 
priorities and outcomes, ensuring that Ethiopia’s 
development is inclusive, equitable, and sustainable.
2.5.2 Partnerships 
Strategic partnerships are essential for the effective 
and efficient implementation of the Cooperation 
Framework and the achievement of its expected 
results. The UN in Ethiopia will engage a wide range of 
partners to ensure local ownership, mobilize resources 
for sustainability, and leverage expertise, lessons 
learned, and good practices. These partnerships will 
align with Ethiopia’s national priorities, including the 
Home-Grown Economic Reform Program (HGERP) 
and the TYDP 2021–2030, and ensure that no one is 
left behind. Key partnerships include:
1. Government
The UN will partner with the GoE at the federal, sectoral, 
and regional levels to ensure alignment with national 
priorities, increase ownership, and secure domestic 
public resources to support sustainability. Key 
government entities include relevant line ministries, 
sector working groups, and regional state authorities. 
These partnerships will ensure that interventions are 
integrated into national systems and contribute to 
long-term development goals.
2. Independent Institutions
The UN will collaborate with independent institutions 
established by the GoE, which play a critical role 
in governance, accountability, and transitional 
justice. These include the EHRC, the Institution of 
the Ombudsman, the Ethiopian National Dialogue 
Commission (ENDC), and the upcoming independent 
institutions under the transitional justice framework, 
such as the Special Bench, the Special Prosecutor’s 
Office, the Truth and Dignity Commission, and the 
Vetting Commission. These institutions will be 
instrumental in promoting human rights, justice, and 
reconciliation.

Partnerships with CSOs, particularly women- and 
youth-focused organizations and grassroots groups, 
will strengthen links with communities, support 
feedback loops, and empower individuals to access 
their rights and opportunities. Social partners, 
including workers’ and employers’ organizations

collaboration with IFIs, with agricultural development

strategy, the UN will work with IFIs to advance climateresilient agricultural practices, improve access to

market linkages. These efforts will contribute to 
broader resilience-building goals, including economic 
diversification, sustainable livelihoods, and food 
security.

governments, community-based organizations, and 
grassroots actors, localization fosters inclusive 
governance, strengthens local ownership, and 
ensures that no one and no place is left behind.
The UN in Ethiopia will work to strengthen local 
governance by building the capacity of local 
institutions to deliver inclusive and effective services. 
Localization efforts will also focus on encouraging 
local governments to adopt Voluntary Local Reviews, 
which serve as a powerful tool for monitoring and 
reporting on SDG progress at the local level. These 
reviews will foster accountability and accelerate the 
implementation of development initiatives tailored to 
the unique contexts of Ethiopia’s regions.
Community engagement will be central to the 
localization agenda, with the UN partnering with local 
actors to co-design and implement development 
initiatives that are responsive to the needs and 
aspirations of communities. This approach will ensure 
that development efforts are rooted in local realities 
and priorities, enhancing their relevance and impact. 
Furthermore, the UN will support the collection and 
analysis of disaggregated data to inform evidencebased policymaking and programming, enabling 
targeted interventions that address inequalities and 
promote inclusive development.
Localization aligns closely with the principle of LNOB 
by addressing systemic barriers and ensuring that 
development efforts reach the most marginalized 
and vulnerable communities. Through localized 
approaches, the Cooperation Framework will enhance 
resilience, promote sustainability, and contribute to 
Ethiopia’s broader development goals, ensuring that 
no one and no place is left behind in the country’s 
journey toward sustainable development.

analysis, and programming to integrate HDP
