2.5.7 Regional Dimensions
Ethiopia’s development challenges are deeply 
interconnected with those of the broader Horn of Africa 
region. Cross-border issues such as migration, trade, 
climate change, and conflict require collaborative 
solutions that transcend national boundaries. The 
Cooperation Framework recognizes the importance 
of regional dimensions in fostering stability, resilience, 
and sustainable development.
Regional collaboration is particularly critical in 
areas such as peacebuilding, DRM, and economic 
integration. Cross-border initiatives, such as joint 
peacebuilding efforts and regional trade facilitation, 
are essential for addressing shared challenges and 
promoting stability. For example, regional dialogues 
can address migration flows and climate-induced 
displacement, while coordinated trade policies can 
enhance economic opportunities and reduce tensions 
in border areas.
The Cooperation Framework aligns with regional 
strategies and frameworks, including those of 
the AU, IGAD, and other sub-regional bodies. 60 UNSDCF ETHIOPIA 2025-2030 UNSDCF ETHIOPIA 2025-2030 61
In particular, the Horn of Africa Initiative (HoAI), where 
Ethiopia is a key member under the leadership of the 
Ministry of Finance, provides a practical platform for 
collaboration. Supported by development partners 
such as the World Bank, AfDB, European Union, and 
bilateral partners, the HoAI has mobilized significant 
investments to address shared regional challenges. 
The UN will work within this existing initiative to 
enhance synergies, align efforts, and jointly invest in 
sustainable solutions.
By addressing regional dimensions, the Cooperation

but also contributes to the stability and prosperity of 
the Horn of Africa. This integrated approach ensures 
that Ethiopia’s development challenges are addressed 
in a way that promotes regional collaboration and 
shared progress.
2.5.8 Critical Assumptions
The successful implementation of the Cooperation 
Framework is based on several critical assumptions 
that reflect the enabling environment required to achieve 
the expected results. These assumptions provide the 
foundation for the Cooperation Framework’s success 
and will guide its implementation and monitoring.
A key assumption is the presence of strong political 
will and commitment to implement governance, 
economic, social, and environmental reforms. 
This includes the government’s willingness 
to uphold human rights, promote inclusive 
governance, and address systemic inequalities.
Macroeconomic stability is also critical, as consistent 
development funding and a stable economic 
environment are necessary to ensure that financial 
resources are sufficient and retain their value 
throughout the Cooperation Framework period. A 
secure and safe environment, as well as reliable 
infrastructure, is essential for the implementation 
of activities. Disruptions to safety, security, or 
infrastructure could halt operations and adversely 
affect progress.
Adequate resources and partnerships must be 
mobilized to support the framework, including from 
non-traditional donors and private sector actors. 
The UN will work to diversify funding sources and 
leverage innovative financing mechanisms, such as 
climate finance and blended finance models. Civic 
space and freedom of expression must also be 
protected, enabling meaningful citizen engagement 
and participation in decision-making processes. 
Institutional and community ownership is critical, 
with national and sub-national institutions, as well 
as community-based organizations, driving and 
sustaining planned interventions. The private sector 
must remain actively engaged in supporting economic 
transformation, renewable energy, and other key 
initiatives.
Finally, the Cooperation Framework must remain 
flexible and adaptive to respond to unforeseen 
shocks, such as natural disasters, economic crises, 
or political instability. This flexibility will be achieved 
through regular monitoring of preparedness, 
occurrence, and response to shocks, guided by 
indicators outlined in the Results and Resource 
Framework. Contingency planning will enable the 
adaptation of strategies and interventions based on 
risk assessments. By proactively addressing risks, 
the Cooperation Framework will remain resilient to 
external disruptions and focused on achieving its 
expected results.

dynamic needs of the country. This ensures that

living framework, capable of addressing Ethiopia’s

3.1 Governance and Management of 
the Cooperation Framework
The implementation of the UNSDCF 2025-2030 is 
guided by a robust and coherent system that ensures 
accountability, inclusivity, and alignment with the 2030 
Agenda for Sustainable Development. Anchored in 
the principles of the Management and Accountability 
Framework, the UNSDCF operationalizes a dual 
accountability system, with the Resident Coordinator 
providing strategic leadership and UN entities working 
collaboratively to deliver results. This framework 
emphasizes evidence-based decision-making, 
results-based management, and the use of data to 
track progress and address challenges effectively. By 
fostering strong partnerships, promoting innovation, 
and prioritizing the needs of the most vulnerable, the 
UNSDCF implementation framework ensures that 
no one is left behind in Ethiopia’s journey toward 
sustainable and inclusive development.
The UNSDCF serves as the most important 
instrument for the planning and implementation of UN 
development activities in Ethiopia. It is the foundation 
from which the specific country programmes of 
individual UN entities are derived, ensuring coherence 
and alignment with national priorities and the SDGs. 
The derivation of country programmes from the 
UNSDCF ensures that all UN entities contribute 
to shared results and impact, while maintaining 
accountability to their respective mandates. This 
process is facilitated by the Resident Coordinator, with 
inclusive participation from the UNCT, civil society, 
and relevant state institutions, ensuring alignment 
with the principles of the UN Charter and international 
norms and standards.
On the derivation of country programmes from the 
Cooperation Framework, three agencies (UNICEF, 
UNDP, and UN Women) opted for Option B, committing 
to develop entity-specific country programmes with 
outcomes copied verbatim from the Framework. 
Five agencies (FAO, ILO, UNESCO, UNDRR, and 
WFP) chose Option C, adopting the Cooperation 
Framework outcomes verbatim while also adding 
agency-specific outcomes. UN agencies that did not 
select these options will submit their programming 
instruments for validation to ensure alignment with 
the Cooperation Framework.
To ensure coherent, coordinated, efficient, and 
effective implementation of strategic priorities, the UN 
– in partnership with the GoE – will use the following 
governance framework:
Guidance and Oversight
The overall responsibility for the UNSDCF will lie with 
the Minister of Finance, on behalf of the GoE and 
the UN Resident Coordinator. The joint Policy and 
Oversight Board (POB) will provide strategic direction 
and oversight of the Cooperation Framework. Cochaired by the Resident Coordinator and the Minister 
of Finance, the POB will include representatives 
from line ministries, government agencies, UN 
entities (both resident and non-resident), and key 
development partners, including bilateral donors and 
selected CSOs. The POB will ensure alignment with 
national, regional, and international frameworks, 
including Ethiopia’s Vision 2030, the Voluntary 
National Review, and the Universal Periodic Review. 
It will monitor implementation progress, review and 
approve the One UN annual progress report, and 
support resource mobilization efforts. The POB will 
meet at least annually to review the Cooperation 
Framework’s performance and provide strategic 
guidance.
Internal Coordination 
The UNCT, chaired by the Resident Coordinator, 
will oversee the day-to-day implementation of the 
Cooperation Framework. Comprising all 25 UN 
entities operating in Ethiopia, the UNCT will include 
non-resident agencies, which will participate 
virtually and in-person during key review processes. 
The UNCT will be responsible for developing 
and approving annual Joint Work Plans (JWPs), 
monitoring and reporting on implementation 
progress, and coordinating resource mobilization 
efforts to ensure coherence and reduce competition 
among UN entities. The Resident Coordinator will 
review and confirm the alignment of all agency 
programming instruments with the Cooperation 
Framework before submission to respective 
headquarters and governing bodies.
The UN Resident Coordinator Office (UNRCO) offers 
administrative, secretariat, and coordination support 
for the UNCT agenda. In partnership with the Ministry 
of Finance, the UNRCO also facilitates operational 
assistance for the effective functioning of the POB. 
Furthermore, the UNRCO team provides oversight and 
coordination support to the secretariats of the results 
groups. They are also represented in all facilitation 
teams, the operations management team, and the 
communications group, primarily for coordination 
and reporting purposes. 68 UNSDCF ETHIOPIA 2025-2030 UNSDCF ETHIOPIA 2025-2030 69
The Programme Management Team (PMT) provides 
advice and inputs for decision-making at UNCT level 
on all matters pertaining to UNSDCF programming, 
encompassing planning, implementation, monitoring 
and evaluation systems and processes in Ethiopia. 
Chaired by one Agency, the PMT is composed 
of deputy representatives/directors, heads of 
programmes/most senior programme staff from 
each of the UN agencies engaged in the UNSDCF. It 
is responsible for overseeing the identification and 
implementation of Joint Programmes (JPs) and

The RGs are integral to ensuring a coordinated and

3.2 Resourcing the Cooperation 
Framework
The UNCT will adopt a joint approach to resource 
mobilization, promoting greater coordination and 
collaboration among UN entities to reduce competition 
and maximize impact. A comprehensive budget for 
the Cooperation Framework will be developed, based 
on the Results and Resources Framework, to ensure 
that resources are allocated strategically to achieve 
the desired outcomes.
Ethiopia’s challenging macroeconomic environment, 
compounded by interconnected crises, has strained 
the country’s fiscal capacity and hindered its ability 
to achieve sustainable development. According 
to the African Development Bank’s 2024 African 
Economic Outlook, Ethiopia requires approximately 
USD 25.8 billion annually to accelerate its structural 
transformation agenda and achieve the SDGs. 
However, declining external assistance, rising 
humanitarian needs, and persistent economic 
challenges have created significant financing gaps.
To address these challenges, the UNCT will support 
the GoE in reforming its development financial 
architecture, including the implementation of the 
Integrated National Financing Framework (INFF). The 
INFF emphasizes sustainable financing pathways that 
reduce reliance on official development assistance 
(ODA) and humanitarian funding, while promoting 
public-private partnerships, catalytic development 
assistance, and market-based solutions. In alignment 
with the UN Funding Compact and the Pact for the 
Future, the UN will work with the Government to secure 
additional financing from diverse mechanisms, foster 
joint resource mobilization, and support domestic 
resource mobilization efforts.
Traditional ODA, while declining, remains a critical 
source of financing for Ethiopia. The UN will 
strengthen data collection and accountability 
mechanisms to improve the allocation and 
efficiency of development assistance. By leveraging 
platforms such as UNINFO and the Ministry of 
Finance’s Aid Management Platform, the UN will 
ensure that resources are effectively directed 
toward priority development needs. Additionally, 
the UN will support the Government in mobilizing 
domestic resources, particularly in the agricultural 
sector, which employs the majority of the 
population and is a key driver of food security and 
economic growth. Efforts will focus on agricultural 
commercialization, market development, and value 
chain transformation, in alignment with Ethiopia’s 
Food Systems Strategy.
The private sector will also play a critical role 
in financing the outcomes of the Cooperation 
Framework. The UN will engage with private sector 
actors to promote sustainable investments in priority 
areas such as renewable energy, agriculture, and youth 
development. The establishment of the Ethiopian 
Securities Exchange presents an opportunity to 
support sustainable capital markets and impact 
investing. The UN will advocate for environmental, 
social, and governance disclosure requirements for 
listed companies and will work with the private sector 
to unlock market-based solutions to sustainable 
development challenges.
Ethiopia’s potential to mobilize climate finance is 
significant, given its success in securing grants from 
multilateral funds such as the Green Climate Fund 
(GCF) and the Global Environment Facility. The UN 
will support the Government in accessing additional 
climate finance, establishing carbon markets, 
and integrating climate action with economic 
development. As the Secretariat for the Climate 
Resilience and Green Energy Forum, the UN will 
coordinate stakeholders, track climate finance, and 
advocate for climate-smart investments.
The GoE will support the UN system agencies’ efforts 
to raise the funds required to meet the needs of this 
Cooperation Framework. In this regard, the Government 
will cooperate with the UN system agencies by 
encouraging potential donor Governments to make 
available the funds needed to implement unfunded 
components of the programme. Furthermore, the 
Government will endorse the UN system agencies’ 
efforts to raise funds for the programme from 
other sources, including the private sector both 
internationally and in Ethiopia. Contributions from 
individuals, corporations, and foundations in Ethiopia 
to support this programme will be permitted and will 
be tax-exempt for the donor, to the maximum extent 
permissible under applicable law.

Planning: Joint Work Plans and Joint 
Programmes
The implementation of the Cooperation Framework 
will be operationalized through JWPs and JPs, which 
serve as key mechanisms for fostering collaboration 
and delivering results. Each Results Group will develop 
a JWP that outlines activities, expected results, 
responsible UN entities, and indicative budgets. These 
plans will be updated annually to reflect evolving 
country contexts and ensure responsiveness to 
emerging challenges and opportunities. Both resident 
and non-resident agencies will contribute to JWPs, 
with non-resident agencies participating virtually and 
during key review processes. Monitoring and reporting 
of JWPs and Results Framework indicators will be 
conducted through UNINFO, ensuring consistency 
and transparency. 
Under the new Cooperation Framework, joint 
programming will be prioritized as a key approach to 
reduce fragmentation, eliminate overlap, and enhance 
alignment and efficiency across UN interventions. By 
fostering greater collaboration among UN entities 
and national partners, joint programming will ensure 
the best use of increasingly limited resources while 
delivering results at scale. This approach will focus 
on achieving transformative change by addressing 
complex, multidimensional challenges through 
integrated and innovative solutions.
A central focus of joint programming will be the 
operationalization of the HDP nexus to address 
the root causes of humanitarian needs, strengthen 
resilience, and reduce aid dependency by 2030. 
By targeting key drivers of vulnerability—such as 
food insecurity, climate shocks, displacement, and 
conflict—JPs will aim to build sustainable systems 
and capacities that reduce the need for humanitarian 
assistance over time. This will include fostering 
social cohesion, promoting inclusive governance, and 
supporting livelihoods to create a foundation for longterm peace and development.

The Cooperation Framework adopts a

stability, macroeconomic and financing trends, and 
the occurrence, preparedness, and response to

collaboration with national partners. This plan 
will outline objectives, methodologies, roles, and 
responsibilities for monitoring and evaluation 
activities, ensuring alignment among stakeholders. 
The MEL Group will lead the implementation of the 
MELP, providing technical support to Results Groups 
and engaging thematic working groups, including 
the Data and Statistics Working Group.
Key components of the MEL framework include:
1. Annual Monitoring and Reviews: Annual 
monitoring and review processes will assess 
progress toward planned results. Data 
collected through the Results Framework will 
be disaggregated by gender, age, disability, 
geographic location, and other dimensions. 
The UNCT will prepare an Annual Results 
Report in collaboration with Results Groups 
and the MEL Group, which will be presented to 
the Policy and Oversight Board for review and 
strategic guidance.
2. Joint Monitoring Visits: Regular joint 
monitoring visits will be conducted to assess 
on-the-ground progress, identify risks, and 
strategize improvements. These visits will 
involve government partners, development 
partners, and other stakeholders, with findings 
documented and shared to inform future 
programming.
3. Data Collection and Analysis: The MEL 
framework will prioritize innovative 
approaches to data collection and analysis, 
leveraging both qualitative and quantitative 
methods. Collaboration with the Data and 
Statistics Working Group will address data 
gaps and strengthen national data systems, 
such as the Civil Registration and Vital 
Statistics (CRVS) system, census data, and 
population surveys. Advanced technologies, 
including artificial intelligence and remote 
sensing, will be explored to enhance data 
quality and analysis.
4. Learning and Capacity Building: Lessons 
learned from monitoring and evaluation 
activities will be documented and shared 
through knowledge products, experiencesharing platforms, and capacity-building 
initiatives. The UNCT will also support the GoE 
in implementing national monitoring and 
evaluation capacity development plans, 
ensuring alignment with the SDGs and 
Ethiopia’s development priorities.
5. Evaluation: A final independent evaluation of 
the Cooperation Framework will be conducted 
in the penultimate year of its implementation 
to assess its overall impact and provide 
recommendations for the next cycle. Midterm reviews and thematic evaluations will 
also be conducted as needed to inform 
adaptive management and ensure inclusivity 
and ownership.
The MEL framework will be implemented in close 
collaboration with national partners to ensure 
alignment with Ethiopia’s development priorities 
and build institutional capacity. By enhancing the 
availability and accessibility of high-quality data, 
the MEL framework will enable evidence-based 
decision-making and contribute to the achievement 
of Ethiopia’s Vision 2030 and the SDGs.
3.4 Risk Management Strategy
Ethiopia’s development journey is shaped by a 
complex and dynamic risk landscape, characterized 
by conflict, climate-induced disasters, economic 
instability, governance deficits, and entrenched 
social inequalities. These risks, identified in the 
CCA and lessons learned from the 2020–2025 
UNSDCF, pose significant challenges to achieving 
the SDGs and Ethiopia’s TYDP. To address these 
challenges, the UNSDCF 2025–2030 integrates 
a comprehensive risk management strategy 
that emphasizes resilience-building, proactive 
mitigation measures, and adaptive management. 
This approach ensures that development gains are 
safeguarded, vulnerabilities are reduced, and no one 
is left behind.
The risks Ethiopia faces are deeply interconnected. 
Conflict and political instability continue to threaten 
peacebuilding efforts and institutional stability, while 
climate-induced disasters such as droughts and 
floods exacerbate food insecurity, displacement, 
and environmental degradation. Economic 
instability, driven by inflation, debt, and limited fiscal

compound these challenges, disproportionately 
affecting women, youth, persons with disabilities, 
and displaced populations. These risks are further 
exacerbated by gaps in data availability and 
institutional capacity, which hinder evidence-based 
decision-making and effective risk monitoring. 
Recognizing these complexities, the UNSDCF adopts a 
holistic and integrated approach to risk management, 
embedding mitigation measures across all strategic 
priorities and outcomes.
Within the Peace and Governance priority, the UNSDCF 
focuses on strengthening early warning systems 
and conflict resolution mechanisms to prevent and 
mitigate conflict at both national and community 
levels. Efforts to build the capacity of governance 
institutions are central to promoting transparency, 
accountability, and inclusive decision-making. 
Transitional justice mechanisms, reconciliation 
processes, and social cohesion initiatives are also 
prioritized to address the root causes of conflict and 
foster lasting peace. These measures are designed 
to create an enabling environment for sustainable 
development, where trust in institutions is restored, 
and communities are empowered to participate in 
governance processes.
In the area of Economy, Food Systems, and Energy, 
the UNSDCF promotes economic diversification to 
reduce reliance on vulnerable sectors such as rainfed agriculture. Investments in green jobs, renewable 
energy, and sustainable agriculture are key to building 
a more resilient economy. Climate-smart agricultural 
practices, including the adoption of droughtresistant crops, irrigation systems, and risk financing 
mechanisms such as crop insurance, are scaled up 
to enhance food security and reduce vulnerabilities to 
climate shocks. To ensure sustainable energy access, 
the framework de-risks investments in renewable 
energy through public-private partnerships and 
regulatory reforms, fostering a transition to affordable 
and clean energy for all.
The Social Services and Protection priority emphasizes 
the need to strengthen health, education, and social 
protection systems to be shock-responsive and 
resilient to crises such as pandemics, displacement, 
and natural disasters. Addressing systemic barriers 
to accessing services is critical to ensuring that 
marginalized groups, including women, children, and

persons with disabilities, are not left behind. Genderresponsive and inclusive service delivery is prioritized, 
alongside investments in robust data systems to 
monitor vulnerabilities and target interventions 
effectively. These efforts aim to build human capital 
and create a foundation for equitable and inclusive 
development.
Under the Environmental Sustainability, Resilience, 
and Preparedness priority, the UNSDCF enhances DRM 
systems by strengthening multi-hazard early warning 
systems and integrating disaster preparedness 
into national and sub-national development plans. 
Community-based disaster preparedness and 
response capacities are also bolstered to ensure that 
vulnerable populations are protected from climateinduced disasters and environmental crises. The 
framework aims to mobilize climate finance through 
mechanisms such as the GCF and carbon markets 
to support climate-resilient infrastructure and naturebased solutions. Sustainable natural resource 
management and circular economy approaches are 
promoted to mitigate environmental degradation and 
reduce vulnerabilities.
The Gender Equality and Empowerment priority 
addresses systemic barriers and long-standing 
discriminatory social norms that perpetuate gender 
inequalities. Prevention and response systems for 
GBV are strengthened, including the establishment 
of safe spaces, legal aid, and psychosocial support 
for survivors. Women’s access to land, finance, and 
markets is supported to enhance their economic 
resilience and reduce inequalities. Investments 
in education, skills development, and leadership 
programs for youth and women are also prioritized 
to foster their full participation in society and ensure 
that they can contribute meaningfully to Ethiopia’s 
development.
In addition to these priority-specific measures, the 
UNSDCF adopts several cross-cutting approaches 
to risk mitigation. The HDP nexus is operationalized 
to address the root causes of vulnerability, 
reduce aid dependency, and build resilience. This 
includes advancing durable solutions for IDPs and 
refugees, ensuring their safe and voluntary return, 
reintegration, or local integration. Localization 
and community engagement are central to the 
framework, empowering local governments and 
community-based organizations to lead risk 
mitigation efforts and ensuring that interventions 
are context-specific and sustainable. Data and 
digital solutions are leveraged to monitor risks, 
track progress, and inform adaptive management, 
while partnerships with the private sector, civil 
society, and IFIs pool resources and expertise for 
risk mitigation.
To ensure that risks are effectively managed throughout 
the implementation period, the UNSDCF incorporates 
robust monitoring and adaptive management 
mechanisms. A risk monitoring framework, integrated 
into the MEL Plan, tracks key risks such as political 
stability, climate shocks, and economic trends. 
Indicators are disaggregated by gender, age, and 
other dimensions to ensure inclusivity. Regular 
scenario planning exercises anticipate emerging risks 
and inform adaptive strategies, enabling the UNCT to 
respond proactively to changing contexts. Lessons 
learned from risk mitigation efforts are documented 
and shared through knowledge products and capacitybuilding initiatives, ensuring that interventions remain 
responsive to evolving risks.
The governance structures of the UNSDCF play a 
central role in overseeing risk management. The 
Policy and Oversight Board 4 provides strategic 
oversight, ensuring alignment with national priorities 
and the 2030 Agenda. Results Groups integrate risk 
mitigation into their JWPs and report on progress 
through the MEL framework, while the Monitoring, 
Evaluation, and Learning Group tracks risks and 
recommends adaptive measures to address 
emerging challenges.
By embedding risk mitigation measures into the 
UNSDCF’s strategic priorities and outcomes, the 
framework ensures that Ethiopia’s development 
efforts are resilient, inclusive, and sustainable. This 
comprehensive risk management strategy not only 
addresses immediate challenges but also builds 
the foundation for long-term stability and prosperity, 
ensuring that no one is left behind in Ethiopia’s journey 
toward sustainable development
3.5 Business Operations Strategy in 
Support of the Cooperation Framework
The BOS under the new Cooperation Framework 
will play a pivotal role in enhancing cost-efficiency, 
reducing duplication, and improving the quality of 
business operations to support programme delivery. 
Aligned with the UN Secretary-General’s efficiency 
agenda and the principles of UN 2.0, the BOS will 
focus on transformational change in the management 
of back-office functions, ensuring that resources 
are optimized to achieve maximum impact at the 
country level.78 UNSDCF ETHIOPIA 2025-2030 UNSDCF ETHIOPIA 2025-2030 79
Building on lessons learned from the current BOS 
framework, a new BOS will be developed by the end of 
2025. This updated strategy will reflect the evolving 
needs of Ethiopia and the UNCT, ensuring that 
business operations are more efficient, innovative, 
and aligned with national priorities. The new BOS will 
prioritize the following key strategies:
1. Cost-Efficiency and Harmonization: By 
consolidating support services and leveraging 
economies of scale, the BOS will reduce 
administrative and transaction costs. This 
includes the establishment of Common Back 
Offices and shared service platforms to 
streamline operations and eliminate 
duplication across UN entities.
2. Common Premises: The co-location of UN 
agencies under common premises will 
enhance collaboration, reduce operational 
costs, and promote a unified presence at both 
national and sub-national levels.
3. Innovation and Digital Transformation: The 
BOS will integrate innovative technologies 
and digital solutions to modernize business 
processes, improve service delivery, and 
enhance data-driven decision-making.
4. Mutual Recognition: The BOS will adopt the 
principle of mutual recognition, enabling UN 
entities to access and utilize each other’s 
policies, procedures, and assets, thereby 
reducing inefficiencies and fostering 
collaboration.
The new BOS will also align with the UN’s commitment 
to the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development 
by ensuring that business operations are not only 
efficient but also environmentally sustainable. This 
includes adopting green practices in procurement, 
energy use, and waste management to minimize the 
environmental footprint of UN operations.
The BOS will directly contribute to Ethiopia’s 
development priorities by ensuring that resources 
are effectively channelled toward programme 
implementation. By reducing operational 
inefficiencies, the BOS will free up resources to 
address critical development challenges. 
The new BOS will be developed through a consultative 
process, incorporating lessons learned from the 
current framework and best practices from other 
countries. It will include a results-based framework 
with clear targets, cost-benefit analyses, and regular 
monitoring and reporting. The UNCT will work 
collaboratively with national partners to ensure that 
the BOS is responsive to Ethiopia’s evolving needs 
and priorities.
By adopting the new BOS, the UNCT in Ethiopia will 
demonstrate its commitment to delivering results 
at scale, achieving greater value for money, and 
supporting the country’s long-term development 
goals in a cost-effective and sustainable manner.
3.6 Protection of Sexual Exploitation 
and Abuse
Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse 
(PSEA) is a key priority for the UNCT entities, 
with a special focus on prioritizing victims’ rights 
and creating an environment in which sexual 
exploitation and abuse (SEA) do not occur. SEA 
is unacceptable behavior and is prohibited for UN 
personnel and UN implementing partners. The 
UNCT in Ethiopia has endorsed a Statement of 
Commitment on PSEA which is signed by all Heads 
of Agencies; all new incoming representatives are 
also briefed and expected to sign the Statement. 
The UNCT entities will also pursue all appropriate 
means to protect against, prevent and respond to 
SEA, and will require a similar commitment from its 
partners. In delivering on the obligations articulated 
in the present Cooperation Framework, the UNCT 
and the GoE affirm their commitment to preventing 
and responding to reports of SEA in connection 
with their personnel involved in joint projects. It 
is understood that this would entail the need to: 
(i) adhere to common values on PSEA, (ii) take 
preventative measures against SEA, (iii) investigate 
allegations, and (iv) take appropriate corrective 
action when incidents occur, including providing 
support to victims in accordance with a victim 
centred approach. The UNCT will provide technical 
support to government institutions to strengthen 
SEA prevention and response systems.
